one_liner: FP16 x INT4 weight-only GEMM for Ampere/Ada GPUs; near-ideal 3.9x over FP16 torch.matmul up to batch 16-32.
what_it_does: A single CUDA kernel that multiplies FP16 activations (m x k) by 4-bit symmetric-quantised weights (k x n) with per-output-channel or group-128 FP16 scales, for the linear layers of LLM decoding. It ships as a PyTorch extension: marlin.Layer replaces an nn.Linear after Layer.pack() converts fake-quantised FP16 weights plus scales into Marlin's reshuffled format, and marlin.mul() calls the kernel directly on pre-packed tensors. The kernel file marlin_cuda_kernel.cu depends only on base CUDA, so it can be dropped into other engines; a GPTQ variant in gptq/ produces Marlin-format Llama-2 checkpoints.
how_it_is_fast: It is built to stay memory-bound on weights up to larger batches: weights are streamed with cp.async and an L2 evict_first cache policy, activations stay in L2 and registers, and shared-memory tiles are double-buffered in a 4-stage pipeline so loads overlap compute. Weights and scales are permuted offline so int4 values dequantise (via LOP3 bit tricks) directly into mma.sync m16n8k16 tensor-core fragments loaded with conflict-free ldmatrix. A 'striped' partitioning gives each SM a contiguous run of tiles that may span several column slices, keeping all SMs busy on realistic shapes, and the cross-block reduction happens in the L2-resident output buffer guarded by global locks.
when_to_use: Decode-phase LLM inference with 4-bit GPTQ-style weights on A10, A100, A6000, RTX 3090/4090-class GPUs at 1-32 tokens per step, where the weight read dominates.
Batched serving, speculative decoding or multi-sample schemes that push the effective batch to 16-32, where older 4-bit kernels (exllamav2, AWQ, bitsandbytes) fall below FP16 speed.
Embedding a dependency-free FP16xINT4 GEMM in a custom C++/CUDA inference engine (one .cu file, plain pointers plus a stream).
Fitting larger models in GPU memory: 4-bit weights with group-128 scales use about 4.125 bits per weight instead of 16.
when_not_to_use: Prefill or large batches: the README plots fall to about 1.55x at batch 128 (about 1.0x at locked base clock), and issue #21 reports 0.82x of FP16 on an A6000 Ada at 16x1024 = 16384 rows.
Hopper or Blackwell GPUs: the README says it is not optimised for Hopper; open issues report failures on RTX 5090 (#40) and an nvcc 13.1 ptxas miscompile of the cp.async cache hint on sm_90 (#44).

Formats it does not cover: BF16 activations, asymmetric or zero-point quantisation (AWQ format), bias, group sizes other than 128 or per-channel, other bit widths; layer dims must have in_features % 128 == 0 and out_features % 256 == 0.
Volta, Turing, AMD or CPU targets: it needs compute capability 8.0 or newer, and a ROCm port request (#43) is open.
Correctness-critical group-128 inference on small GPUs until issue #45 is resolved (see gotchas).

integration.form: PyTorch CUDA extension (pip install . from source, no wheel) or source-drop of marlin/marlin_cuda_kernel.cu
integration.dependencies: kernel: CUDA runtime only; Python wrapper: torch >= 2.0, numpy; GPTQ example: transformers, datasets, sentencepiece
integration.min_toolchain: CUDA >= 11.8 with nvcc matching torch's CUDA; C++ standard and flags are torch CUDAExtension defaults (not stated)
integration.platforms: NVIDIA compute capability >= 8.0 (Ampere, Ada); Hopper works but is not optimised; Linux assumed (not stated)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each call needs a zeroed int workspace that the kernel uses as cross-block lock storage, and a marlin.Layer owns one, so concurrent launches sharing a layer's workspace on different streams are not covered
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — marlin.Layer replaces nn.Linear (no bias) after packing fake-quantised FP16 weights and scales; it is a 4-bit approximation of the FP16 matmul, not a bit-exact replacement

gotchas: Issue #45 (2026-09-29, unanswered) reports wrong and non-deterministic outputs with groupsize 128 at Llama-2-7B shapes (m=300) on a Jetson Orin Nano (8 SMs), relative errors 1.3e-3 to 2e-2 with whole 64-row blocks corrupted, while per-channel scales stay correct; in test.py, test_llama_shapes starts with a bare return, so the repository's own tests never run those shapes.

Issue #42 reports a possible async race where the per-channel scale load (cp_async4_stream) followed by thread_block_reduce leaves sh_s zeroed; #27 and #38 report slight non-determinism and batch-size-dependent results. None has a maintainer reply.
Split-k reduction downcasts FP32 accumulators to FP16 in the output buffer, so results depend on how tiles are partitioned across SMs.
The README benchmarks ran with ECC disabled on the A10 (10-15% more bandwidth), and bench.py times 10 launches with time.time without synchronising between them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Marlin over BitBLAS when you only need FP16xINT4 on Ampere/Ada and want one small kernel file with no TVM-based tuning stack; pick BitBLAS for INT2/INT1/FP4 or mixed formats. For CPU inference of low-bit models use T-MAC, BitNet or ik_llama.cpp instead; for production serving use vLLM's maintained Marlin fork (gptq_marlin, awq_marlin) rather than this frozen repo.
verified_claims_summary: First-party plots only: on an NVIDIA A10 with ECC disabled, a 72k x 18k group-128 matmul ran about 3.87-3.9x faster than FP16 torch.matmul at batch 1-16, 3.1x at 64 and 1.55x at 128 (about 1.0x at 128 with clocks locked to base), and the linear layers of Llama and Falcon models at batch 16 ran about 3.4-4.25x faster on A10, 3090 and A6000 and 2.2-3.65x on A100 (approximate plot readings, derived from page data); compiler flags and host CPU are not stated. One user report (#21, A6000 Ada) measured 1.16x at 1024 rows and 0.82x at 16384 rows.
status_note: Stale research code (14 commits, last 2024-09-04, 34 open issues mostly unanswered) under Apache-2.0; the kernel is easy to vendor, but the maintained descendants live in vLLM, and the open correctness reports (#45, #42) should be checked against your shapes before use.
